questions.q: Why does the BookStore API start with no framework at all?
questions.explain: Routing, JSON bodies, errors, validation: you write each one yourself. At the end of the three lessons you list what hurts. Type-safe API layers fixes part of that list with typed layers; the rest is the reason frameworks, and ZudoJS, exist.
options: Because frameworks do not work with TypeScript
So you write every job a framework does by hand, and see why frameworks exist
Because a server without a framework is always faster and safer
Because Node.js cannot install frameworks without a database

questions.q: What does npm pkg set type=module do for the BookStore project?
questions.explain: Without "type": "module", Node.js treats .js files as CommonJS. The whole course uses ES modules with import and export.
options: It installs TypeScript
It adds "type": "module" to package.json, so .js files are ES modules and import works
It makes the package private
It creates the src/ folder

questions.q: The scripts are "dev": "tsx watch src/server.ts", "start": "tsx src/server.ts" and "typecheck": "tsc --noEmit". Which is true?
questions.explain: tsx runs TypeScript without checking types; watch makes it restart on every change. Type errors are found by npm run typecheck, which is tsc --noEmit: check, write nothing.
options: start checks the types before running
dev restarts the server when you save a file; typecheck only checks types and runs nothing
typecheck builds a dist/ folder
dev and start both check types first

questions.q: The port, the database address and secrets can differ between your laptop and a server. Where should they come from?
questions.explain: Configuration never goes into the code. It comes from process.env. One module reads it, checks it at startup, and turns it into a typed Config object that everything else uses.
options: Constants at the top of server.ts
Environment variables, read and checked once in config.ts
A config.json committed to Git, with the secrets in it
Query strings on each request

questions.q: Why does loadConfig(env) take the environment as a parameter instead of reading process.env itself?
questions.explain: A function that takes its input as a parameter is easy to test: loadConfig({ PORT: "eighty" }) checks the error case without changing the real environment.
options: Because process.env cannot be read inside a module
So a test can pass any object it likes, while the server passes process.env
Because it makes the port a number automatically
To hide the environment from TypeScript

questions.q: You start the server with PORT=eighty npm start. What should a well-written config.ts do?
questions.explain: This is failing fast. If the server quietly used 3000, the person who set PORT would look for it in the wrong place. A clear error at startup is much easier to fix than a confusing failure later.
options: Quietly use port 3000 so the server still starts
Start on port 80, the closest valid value
Refuse to start, with an error that says PORT is wrong and what it got
Start, and return an error on every request

questions.q: Why do BookStore handlers take a small ApiRequest object and return an ApiResponse, instead of using the node:http request and response?
questions.explain: The node:http objects are big and awkward to fake. A handler that turns plain data into plain data can be called directly in a test, with no server running.
options: Because node:http objects cannot be used in TypeScript
Plain objects are easy to build and test, and only one file (app.ts) has to talk to node:http
Because plain objects are sent faster over the network
So that handlers can write headers directly

questions.q: In ApiRequest, why is body typed unknown and not the shape the route expects?
questions.explain: Any client can send anything. unknown forces the handler to narrow the value with typeof and in before touching a field like body.name.
options: Because TypeScript cannot describe JSON
It comes from outside, so nothing about it is trusted until the handler has checked it
Because every body is a string
Because unknown is faster than an interface

questions.q: type Handler = (request: ApiRequest) => ApiResponse | Promise<ApiResponse>. What does the return type allow?
questions.explain: Simple handlers return { status, body } at once; handlers that wait for a database are async. app.ts writes await match.handler(request), which works for both.
options: Handlers must be async
Handlers may return nothing
A handler may return the response directly, or be async and return a Promise of it
A handler may return either a response or an error

questions.q: A route is registered with the pattern /books/:id. Which path does it match, and what are the params?
questions.explain: A pattern and a path match when they have the same number of parts and every fixed part is equal. A part starting with : matches anything and is saved as a string: every id in a URL is text until you convert it.
options: /books, with { id: '' }
/books/7, with { id: '7' }
/books/7/reviews, with { id: '7' }
/books/7, with { id: 7 }

questions.q: The router has only GET /books/:id. A client sends DELETE /books/1. What should the API answer?
questions.explain: "The path exists, but not with this method" (405) is different from "the path does not exist" (404). That is why match returns three cases, and the 405 message lists the allowed methods.
options: 404 Not Found, because there is no DELETE route
405 Method Not Allowed, because the path exists but not for this method
400 Bad Request
200 OK, with the book

questions.q: match returns a union with kind: "found" | "wrong-method" | "not-found". Why can the code read match.params inside if (match.kind === "found") but not before it?
questions.explain: Only the "found" case has params, and only "wrong-method" has allowed. Checking kind tells TypeScript which case it has, so each field is allowed exactly where it exists.
options: Because params is private until then
Because it is a discriminated union: checking kind narrows it to the case that has params
Because params is created by the if
It can be read anywhere; TypeScript does not check it

questions.q: A handler has a bug, and a TypeError (not an HttpError) reaches toErrorResponse. What does the client get?
questions.explain: An HttpError was thrown on purpose, so its message is safe to show. Anything else is a bug: log it with console.error and send { error: "internal_error" }. A stack trace tells an attacker how your code is built.
options: The error message and stack trace, so it can report the bug
A plain 500 with a generic message; the details go only to the server log
A 400, because the client must have sent something wrong
No answer at all; the connection is closed

questions.q: Why does readJson stop reading after 100,000 bytes and answer 413?
questions.explain: Every chunk is kept in memory until the body is complete. A size limit (413 Content Too Large) protects the server from one client using up all its memory.
options: Because JSON cannot be longer than that
Without a limit, one client could send gigabytes and fill the server's memory
Because JSON.parse is slow on long text
Because HTTP bodies are limited to 100 KB by the protocol

questions.q: You run curl -X POST http://localhost:3000/authors -d 'name=Octavia'. What does the BookStore answer, and why?
questions.explain: readJson refuses any body whose content-type does not start with application/json: 415 Unsupported Media Type. Add -H 'content-type: application/json' and send real JSON.
options: 201, because curl sends JSON by default
400, because the name is too short
415, because curl's -d sends a form, not a body labelled application/json
404, because the path is wrong

questions.q: A client sends {"name": with content-type: application/json. What happens in readJson?
questions.explain: The try/catch around JSON.parse turns broken JSON into a clear 400 Bad Request instead of an unexpected error. The content type was right, so it is not 415.
options: The server crashes, because JSON.parse throws
JSON.parse throws, and readJson turns that into an HttpError 400 invalid_json
The body becomes undefined and the handler runs
415, because the body is not JSON

questions.q: Why does the BookStore store prices as whole cents, like priceCents: 1299 for 12.99?
questions.explain: Whole numbers add up exactly; decimal fractions like 0.1 cannot be stored exactly in a JavaScript number. Keep money in cents and divide by 100 only to display it.
options: Because JSON cannot hold decimal numbers
Because decimals are not exact in JavaScript (0.1 + 0.2 is not exactly 0.3), and money must add up exactly
Because PostgreSQL has no decimal type
To make the numbers shorter

questions.q: Why does toId reject ids above 2_147_483_647?
questions.explain: JavaScript can hold much bigger whole numbers, but the database column cannot. Refusing it at the edge with a clear 400 is better than an odd error from deep inside the database.
options: Because JavaScript numbers cannot go higher
It is the largest integer PostgreSQL can store in an integer column, so checking now avoids a confusing database error later
Because URLs cannot be longer than ten digits
To stop clients from guessing ids

questions.q: What status does POST /authors return when it creates an author?
questions.explain: 201 Created is the status for "I made a new thing". The body is the new author, with the id the server gave it.
options: 200 OK
201 Created
202 Accepted
204 No Content

questions.q: The check script calls createApp(createRouter()).listen(0). What does port 0 mean?
questions.explain: Port 0 lets the operating system pick a free port, so the test never clashes with a server that is already running. server.address() tells you which port it picked.
options: The server listens on no port, for tests only
"Any free port, you choose"; the script reads the real port from server.address()
The default HTTP port, 80
The port from the PORT environment variable

questions.q: Where are thrown errors turned into responses in the BookStore?
questions.explain: Handlers just throw new HttpError(404, …). The single try/catch around the router, body reading and handler turns every error into a status code and a JSON body.
options: In every handler, with its own try/catch
In one try/catch in app.ts, which calls toErrorResponse
In server.ts, with process.on("uncaughtException")
Nowhere: Node.js answers 500 by itself

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: No PORT means the default "3000". "eighty" is not all digits and 70000 is too big, so both fail fast. The message shows the raw text, which is what the person actually typed.
options:
3000 8080
PORT must be a whole number from 0 to 65535, got "eighty"
PORT must be a whole number from 0 to 65535, got "70000"

3000 8080
PORT must be a whole number from 0 to 65535, got "NaN"
PORT must be a whole number from 0 to 65535, got "70000"

undefined 8080
PORT must be a whole number from 0 to 65535, got "eighty"
PORT must be a whole number from 0 to 65535, got "70000"

3000 "8080"
PORT must be a whole number from 0 to 65535, got "eighty"

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: split("/") makes empty strings at the start and end; the filter removes them. So a trailing slash does not change the parts, and / has no parts at all.

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: The : is cut off, so the param is named id, and its value is the string '7'. /books exists for GET and POST but not DELETE, so the router collects both allowed methods for a 405.

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: Only whole numbers from 1 to the PostgreSQL limit pass. Number(undefined) is NaN, which is not an integer. Every id in a URL is a string, so it must be converted and checked like this before use.
options: 7 invalid invalid invalid invalid invalid invalid
7 invalid -5 2.5 0 99999999999 invalid
7 invalid invalid 2 invalid invalid invalid

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: HttpError extends Error, so it is both. Setting this.name makes logs show HttpError. The response body carries the machine-readable code and the human message.
options:
true HttpError 404
{"error":"not_found","message":"Book not found"}

false HttpError 404
{"error":"not_found","message":"Book not found"}

true Error 404
{"error":"not_found","message":"Book not found"}

true HttpError 404
{"error":"HttpError","message":"Book not found"}

questions.q: toErrorResponse gets a logger here so you can see what it logs. What does this print?
questions.explain: An HttpError becomes its own status and a safe message, with nothing logged. Any other error is a bug: its details go only to the server log, and the client gets a generic 500.
options:
{"status":400,"body":{"error":"invalid_id","message":"id must be a number"}}
{"status":500,"body":{"error":"internal_error","message":"db.query is not a function"}}

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: new URL splits the path from the query. Query values are always strings, and a missing one is null, not undefined. That is why the books route checks raw === null and converts with toId.
options:
/books
2 string
null

/books?authorId=2&sort=title
2 string
null

/books
2 number
undefined

http://localhost/books
2 string
null

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: With authorId=1, only that author's books are kept. Without it, raw is null, authorId is undefined, and the filter keeps every book.
options:
[ 'Things Fall Apart', 'No Longer at Ease' ]
3

[ 'Things Fall Apart' ]
3

[ 'Things Fall Apart', 'No Longer at Ease' ]
0

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: Each newId() adds one to the last id, so the third author gets id 3. Map.get returns undefined for a missing key, and the route turns that into a 404.
options: 3 3 undefined
2 3 undefined
3 3 null
1 3 undefined

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: Decimal fractions are not exact in JavaScript. Whole cents add up exactly, and you divide by 100 only when you display the price.

questions.q: sendJson sets content-length with Buffer.byteLength(text). What does this print?
questions.explain: content-length counts bytes, not characters. é is one character but two bytes in UTF-8, so text.length would be one too small and the client would cut off the body.
questions.code:
const text = JSON.stringify({ name: "Chimamanda Ngozi Adichie", city: "Enugu é" });
console.log(text.length, Buffer.byteLength(text));

questions.q: This script starts a tiny server on a free port and calls it. What does it print?
questions.explain: Every answer, even a failure, is a status code and a JSON body with a JSON content type. req.url is only the path and query, with no host, which is why app.ts passes "http://localhost" as the base to new URL.
options:
404 application/json; charset=utf-8
{"error":"not_found","message":"Nothing at /orders"}

200 application/json; charset=utf-8
{"error":"not_found","message":"Nothing at /orders"}

404 text/plain
{"error":"not_found","message":"Nothing at /orders"}

404 application/json; charset=utf-8

questions.q:
Write matchParts(pattern, parts). If the lengths differ, return undefined. A pattern part starting with : matches anything and saves it in params (without the :); any other part must be equal, or return undefined. The program should print:

{ id: '7' }
undefined
undefined
{ authorId: '2', bookId: '9' }
questions.explain: Compare part by part. want.slice(1) drops the : to get the param name. The values stay strings; a route converts them with toId.

questions.q:
Finish Router.match. For each route whose parts match (use the given matchParts): return found if the method is the same, otherwise remember the route's method. After the loop, return wrong-method with the remembered methods, or not-found if there are none. The program should print:

found { id: '7' }
wrong-method [ 'GET', 'POST' ]
not-found
questions.explain: Returning a discriminated union keeps 404 and 405 apart: the path /books exists, just not for PUT, so the answer lists the methods that are allowed.

questions.q:
Write toId(raw, name). Convert raw with Number. If the result is not a whole number from 1 to MAX_ID, throw new HttpError(400, "invalid_id", `${name} must be a whole number from 1 to ${MAX_ID}`). Otherwise return it. The program should print:

7
400 id must be a whole number from 1 to 2147483647
400 authorId must be a whole number from 1 to 2147483647
questions.explain: Every id in a URL is text and could be anything. Number.isInteger refuses NaN and decimals, and the range check refuses 0, negatives and values the database cannot store.
questions.expected:
7
400 id must be a whole number from 1 to 2147483647
400 authorId must be a whole number from 1 to 2147483647

questions.q:
Write loadConfig(env). PORT defaults to "3000". If it is not a whole number from 0 to 65535, throw an Error with the message PORT must be a whole number from 0 to 65535, got "<raw>". Return { port }. The program should print:

{ port: 3000 }
{ port: 8080 }
PORT must be a whole number from 0 to 65535, got "eighty"
questions.explain: Read the environment once, check it, and fail fast with a message that names the setting and the bad value. Because env is a parameter, this runs anywhere, even in the browser.

questions.q:
Write toErrorResponse(error). For an HttpError, return its status and the body { error: code, message }. For anything else, return status 500 and the body { error: "internal_error", message: "Something went wrong" }, never the real message. The program should print:

{"status":404,"body":{"error":"not_found","message":"Book not found"}}
{"status":500,"body":{"error":"internal_error","message":"Something went wrong"}}
{"status":500,"body":{"error":"internal_error","message":"Something went wrong"}}
questions.explain: Only errors you threw on purpose have safe messages. The second message would tell an attacker about your database. In the real errors.ts, that error is also written to the server log with console.error.

questions.q:
Write parseAuthor(body) for POST /authors. body is unknown. If it is not an object with a name, throw new HttpError(400, "invalid_body", "Send an object with a name"). If name is not a non-empty string (after trimming), throw new HttpError(400, "invalid_body", "name must be a non-empty string"). Otherwise return the trimmed name. The program should print:

Octavia E. Butler
Send an object with a name
name must be a non-empty string
name must be a non-empty string
questions.explain: Narrow step by step: typeof and !== null make it an object, "name" in body lets you read body.name as unknown, and the second typeof makes it a string.
questions.expected:
Octavia E. Butler
Send an object with a name
name must be a non-empty string
name must be a non-empty string

questions.q:
Write statusFor(match), the part of app.ts that answers before a handler runs: not-found gives 404 Nothing here, wrong-method gives 405 Use followed by the allowed methods joined with or , and found gives 200 OK. The program should print:

404 Nothing here
405 Use GET or POST
200 OK
questions.explain: A switch on kind narrows each case, so match.allowed is only used where it exists. Because every case returns, TypeScript knows the function always returns a string.
questions.expected:
404 Nothing here
405 Use GET or POST
200 OK

questions.q:
Write listBooks(query) for GET /books. Read authorId from the URLSearchParams. When it is missing, return every book's title; otherwise return the titles of that author's books only. The program should print:

[ 'A Wizard of Earthsea' ]
[ 'Things Fall Apart', 'A Wizard of Earthsea', 'Arrow of God' ]
questions.explain: query.get returns a string or null. Convert the string before comparing: "2" === 2 is false. In the real route, toId does the conversion and also answers 400 for bad input.
questions.expected:
[ 'A Wizard of Earthsea' ]
[ 'Things Fall Apart', 'A Wizard of Earthsea', 'Arrow of God' ]

questions.q:
Finish the generic in-memory Table. newId() returns 1, 2, 3, …; save(row) stores the row by its id and returns it; get(id) returns the row or undefined; all() returns every row. The program should print:

2 [ 'Chinua Achebe', 'Ursula K. Le Guin' ] undefined
questions.explain: T extends { readonly id: number } lets the table read row.id for any row type. A Map keyed by id gives fast lookups, and get returns undefined for a missing id.
